problem: Mobile-manipulation research has lacked a reproducible benchmark that requires picking any object in an unseen, large, multi-room, continuous environment and placing it somewhere. Prior benchmarks simplify the problem with discrete actions, small or closed object sets, or single rooms. They also rarely come with a shared real robot stack, so results cannot be reproduced across labs or transferred from sim to real.
motivation: Open-vocabulary vision-language models such as CLIP and DETIC now let robots generalize beyond fixed categories. However, open-vocab navigation and manipulation results are reported on many different robots and settings and are still limited to single rooms, so they cannot be compared. A standardized task, a matched simulation benchmark and an affordable, reproducible real-robot stack are needed to evaluate integrated systems end to end: perception, navigation and manipulation together.
key_idea: Define Open-Vocabulary Mobile Manipulation ('Move object from start_receptacle to goal_receptacle' with seen and unseen object categories), instantiate it in Habitat on HSSD scenes plus a controlled real apartment, and release HomeRobot, a unified sim/real software stack for the Hello Robot Stretch with modular heuristic and RL baselines.
insight: Perception, not control, is the dominant bottleneck. Replacing ground-truth segmentation with DETIC collapses overall success: for the all-RL pipeline, sim SR drops from 14.8 to 0.4 and partial success from 48.3 to 9.6. The heuristic pipeline degrades less, and its FindObj (28.7) even beats RL FindObj (21.7) under DETIC. The authors attribute this to the 2D semantic map aggregating noisy per-frame detections over time. RL navigation with DETIC also explores less efficiently (about 539 vs 335 FindObj steps) and can 'give up'. With GT perception, the learned Gaze and Place skills help clearly: with heuristic nav, overall SR rises from 5.1 to 13.2 when RL gaze and RL place are used. Seen vs. unseen object categories show little difference because generalization is delegated to the pretrained detector.
method: Task definition (OVMM): the agent gets the names of an object, a start receptacle and a goal receptacle and must find the object on the start receptacle, pick it, find the goal receptacle and place it; success is staged (FindObj → Pick → FindRec → Place), with a partial-success metric averaging the 4 stage successes; 1250-step budget in sim, 300 in the real world.

Simulation benchmark: 60 HSSD scenes in modified Habitat (38 train / 12 val / 10 test), 2,535 objects from 129 categories (AI2-THOR, ABO, Google Scanned Objects, HSSD) split into seen/unseen categories and instances; 21 receptacle categories; procedurally generated navigable/reachable episodes with precomputed receptacle viewpoints; improved PBR + HBAO rendering at about a 3% FPS cost.

HomeRobot stack: identical sim/real Agent/Environment APIs for the Stretch with DexWrist; a GPU workstation runs perception and planning while the robot runs low-level control plus Hector SLAM over ROS; includes a goal-pose velocity controller, navigation vs manipulation modes, and a heuristic top-down voxel grasp policy.
OVMMAgent state machine: calls the FindObj, Gaze, Pick, FindRec and Place skills in sequence; Pick is a magic snap in sim and the heuristic voxel grasp in the real world.

Heuristic baseline: DETIC open-vocabulary segmentation projected into a 2D semantic map (5 cm cells, C+4 channels, from SemExp/Gervet et al.), frontier exploration, a Fast Marching Method planner with start-receptacle-guided object search, and heuristic placement that picks the centre of the largest flat slab of the receptacle point cloud.

RL baseline: four DD-PPO skills (FindObj, FindRec, Gaze, Place) trained in sim on depth, GT semantic segmentation with object-level dropout, CLIP goal embeddings, pose and joint states at 160x120; navigation skills use a discrete action space (0.25 m forward / turns), while Gaze and Place use continuous teleported base/arm/head actions; each skill has a shaped reward (distance, angle, collision and contact terms); at test time DETIC masks replace the GT segmentation.

setting.backbone: RL baseline: DD-PPO skill policies (depth + segmentation masks + CLIP goal embedding, trained from scratch in sim); heuristic baseline: frozen DETIC + semantic map + frontier exploration + FMM planner; both use frozen DETIC for open-vocabulary segmentation at test time
setting.training_data: RL skills trained in Habitat on 38 HSSD train scenes with seen-category/seen-instance objects (85 categories, 1,363 instances), using GT semantic segmentation; the heuristic baseline needs no training (off-the-shelf DETIC)
setting.observation: egocentric head-camera RGB-D (RL policies use depth + segmentation, not raw RGB), pose relative to start (SLAM in real), joint/gripper proprioception, goal names as text/CLIP embedding
setting.action_space: RL nav: discrete FORWARD 0.25 m / fixed in-place turns + STOP; manipulation skills: continuous teleported base (10-25 cm forward, 5-30° turn), head/wrist (0.02-0.1 rad), arm extension/lift (2-10 cm); heuristic: FMM-planned waypoints to a velocity controller; Pick is a high-level action (magic snap in sim)
setting.privileged: GT-perception variants use simulator ground-truth semantic segmentation; in sim, grasping is a magic snap and pose comes from the simulator; DETIC variants use no GT semantics. Real world uses Hector SLAM pose and no prior map.

numbers_note: The simulation split is called 'held-out scenes' in the main text, and the seen/unseen table explicitly says 'from the validation set', so 'val' is assumed. The main table has 8 rows (GT/DETIC × {Heur-nav, RL-nav} × {Heur, RL gaze+place}); the two mixed-skill combinations per perception type are omitted here. With GT perception: Heur nav + RL gaze/place gives SR 13.2 and partial success 40.9; RL nav + Heur place gives SR 7.3 and partial success 42.8. With DETIC: Heur nav + RL gaze/place gives SR 0.5 and partial success 12.2; RL nav + Heur place gives SR 0.6 and partial success 10.0. Table 7 (seen vs unseen) is internally inconsistent for DETIC rows: the 'All' column (e.g., FindObj 28.7, overall 0.4) is higher or lower than both the SC,UI and UC,UI subsets. The number of val episodes is not stated.
results: All baselines are far from solving OVMM. With realistic DETIC perception, overall simulation success is at most 0.6%, while partial success is 12.4 (heuristic) and 9.6 (all-RL). With ground-truth segmentation, the all-RL pipeline reaches 14.8% SR and 48.3 partial success, versus 5.1 / 34.8 for the heuristic pipeline. In the real apartment (20 episodes), the sim-trained RL skills transfer: they reach 20% overall success against 15% for the heuristic baseline, with the gains coming from RL Gaze (Pick 45 vs 35) and more precise placing.
limitations: Grasping is not physically simulated: pick is a 'magic snap' in sim and a separate heuristic grasp policy in the real world. A stricter collision-aware grasp condition gave only 47% collision-free reaches.
There are no full natural-language instructions, and DETIC needs a fixed vocabulary list. Perception errors dominate failures, and sim success with DETIC is under 1%.
The FMM planner models the robot as a cylinder on a 5 cm grid and does not handle dynamic obstacles. The real-world evaluation is small: 20 episodes in a single controlled apartment.
builds_on: Gervet et al. 2022 modular object navigation
compares_to: Internal ablations only: heuristic (DETIC + semantic map + FMM) vs DD-PPO RL skills, with GT vs DETIC perception; no external methods evaluated
